{{short description|Unique ellipse tangent to all 3 midpoints of a given triangle's sides}}
{{CS1 config|mode=cs2}}
[[Image:Steiner Inellipse.svg|250px|right|thumb|
The Steiner inellipse. According to [[Marden's theorem]], given the triangle with vertices {{math|(1, 7), (7, 5), (3, 1)}}, the [[Focus (geometry)|foci]] of the inellipse are {{math|(3, 5)}} and {{math|(13/3, 11/3)}}, since
<math>\begin{align}
& D_x(1+7i-x)(7+5i-x)(3+i-x) \\
& = -3\left(\tfrac{13}{3}+\tfrac{11}{3}i-x\right)(3+5i-x)
\end{align}</math>]] 

In [[geometry]], the '''Steiner inellipse''',<ref name=Weisstein>{{mathworld|title=Steiner Inellipse|id=SteinerInellipse}}</ref> '''midpoint inellipse''', or '''midpoint ellipse''' of a [[triangle]] is the unique [[ellipse]] inscribed in the triangle and [[tangent]] to the sides at their [[midpoint]]s. It is an example of an [[inellipse]]. By comparison the [[inscribed circle]] and [[Mandart inellipse]] of a triangle are other inconics that are tangent to the sides, but not at the midpoints unless the triangle is [[equilateral triangle|equilateral]]. The Steiner inellipse is attributed by Dörrie<ref>{{citation
 | last = Dörrie | first = Heinrich
 | translator-last = Antin | translator-first = David
 | contribution = Steiner's ellipse problem
 | isbn = 978-0-486-61348-2
 | page = 378–381
 | publisher = Dover
 | title = 100 Great Problems of Elementary Mathematics
 | year = 1965}}</ref> to [[Jakob Steiner]], and a proof of its uniqueness is given by Dan Kalman.<ref name=Kalman>{{citation
 |last        = Kalman
 |first       = Dan
 |issue       = 4
 |journal     = [[American Mathematical Monthly]]
 |mr          = 2398412
 |jstor       = 27642475
 |pages       = 330–338
 |title       = An elementary proof of Marden's theorem
 |url         = http://mathdl.maa.org/images/upload_library/22/Ford/Kalman.pdf
 |volume      = 115
 |year        = 2008
 |doi = 10.1080/00029890.2008.11920532
 |url-status     = dead
 |archiveurl  = https://web.archive.org/web/20120826050103/http://mathdl.maa.org/images/upload_library/22/Ford/Kalman.pdf
 |archivedate = 2012-08-26
}}.</ref>

The Steiner inellipse contrasts with the [[Steiner circumellipse]], also called simply the Steiner ellipse, which is the unique ellipse that passes through the vertices of a given triangle and whose center is the triangle's [[centroid]].<ref>{{mathworld|title=Steiner Circumellipse|urlname=SteinerCircumellipse}}</ref>

== Definition and properties ==
;Definition
An ellipse that is tangent to the sides of a triangle {{math|△''ABC''}} at its midpoints <math>M_1,M_2,M_3</math> is called the '''Steiner inellipse''' of {{math|△''ABC''}}.
[[File:Steiner-inellipse-1.svg|thumb|
{{legend-line|solid #333333|Arbitrary triangle {{math|△''ABC''}}}}
{{legend-line|solid blue|Steiner inellipse}}
{{legend-line|solid red|Steiner ellipse}}
{{legend-line|dashed #e053bb 2px|Major and minor axes}}]]
[[File:Steiner-inellipse-0.svg|thumb|
{{legend-line|solid #333333|[[Equilateral triangle]] {{math|△''ABC''}}}}
{{legend-line|solid blue|Steiner inellipse}}
{{legend-line|solid red|Steiner ellipse}}]]
'''Properties:'''<br />
For an arbitrary triangle {{math|△''ABC''}} with midpoints <math>M_1,M_2,M_3</math> of its sides the following statements are true:<br />
a) There ''exists'' exactly one Steiner inellipse.<br />
b) The ''center'' of the Steiner inellipse is the [[centroid]] {{mvar|S}} of {{math|△''ABC''}}.<br>
c1) The triangle <math>\triangle M_1M_2M_3</math> has the same centroid {{mvar|S}} and the Steiner inellipse of {{math|△''ABC''}} is the Steiner ellipse of the triangle <math>\triangle M_1M_2M_3.</math> <br/>
c2) The Steiner inellipse of a triangle is the ''scaled'' Steiner Ellipse with scaling factor 1/2 and the centroid as center. Hence both ellipses have the same [[Eccentricity (mathematics)|eccentricity]], are ''similar''.<br />
d) The ''area'' of the Steiner inellipse is <math>\tfrac{\pi}{3 \sqrt{3}}</math>-times the area of the triangle.<br />
e) The Steiner inellipse has the ''greatest area'' of all inellipses of the triangle.
<ref name=Chakerian>{{citation
 | last = Chakerian | first = G. D.
 | editor-last = Honsberger | editor-first = Ross
 | contribution = A distorted view of geometry
 | location = Washington, D.C.
 | pages = 135–136, 145–146
 | publisher = Mathematical Association of America
 | series = The Dolciani Mathematical Expositions
 | title = Mathematical plums
 | volume = 4
 | year = 1979}}.</ref>{{rp|p.146}}<ref name=Minda/>{{rp|Corollary 4.2}}
;Proof
The proofs of properties a),b),c) are based on the following properties of an affine mapping: 1) any triangle can be considered as an affine image of an equilateral triangle. 2) Midpoints of sides are mapped onto midpoints and centroids on centroids. The center of an ellipse is mapped onto the center of its image.<br>
Hence its suffice to prove properties a),b),c) for an equilateral triangle:<br>
a) To any equilateral triangle there exists an [[Incircle and excircles of a triangle|incircle]]. It touches the sides at its midpoints. There is no other (non-degenerate) conic section with the same properties, because a conic section is determined by 5 points/tangents.<br />
b) By a simple calculation.<br />
c) The [[circumcircle]] is mapped by a scaling, with factor 1/2 and the centroid as center, onto the incircle. The eccentricity is an invariant.<br/>
d) The ratio of areas is invariant to affine transformations. So the ratio can be calculated for the equilateral triangle.<br />
e) See [[Inellipse#Inellipse with the greatest area|Inellipse]].

== Parametric representation and semi-axes ==
'''Parametric representation:'''
* Because a Steiner inellipse of a triangle {{math|△''ABC''}} is a scaled Steiner ellipse (factor 1/2, center is centroid) one gets a parametric representation derived from the trigonometric representation of the [[Steiner ellipse#Parametric representaion and equation|Steiner ellipse]] :
::<math>\vec x =\vec p(t)=\overrightarrow{OS}\; +\; {\color{blue}\frac 1 2 }\overrightarrow{SC}\; \cos t \;+\; \frac{1}{{\color{blue}2}\sqrt{3}}\overrightarrow{AB}\; \sin t \; , \quad 0\le t <2\pi\ .</math>

* The '''4 vertices''' of the Steiner inellipse are
::<math>\vec p(t_0),\; \vec p(t_0\pm\frac{\pi}{2}),\; \vec p(t_0+\pi),</math>
:where {{math|''t''{{sub|0}}}} is the solution of
::<math>\cot (2t_0)= \tfrac{\vec f_1^{\, 2}-\vec f_2^{\, 2}}{2\vec f_1 \cdot \vec f_2}\quad</math> with <math>\quad \vec f_1=\frac 1 2 \vec{SC},\quad \vec f_2=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\vec{AB}\ .</math>

'''Semi-axes:'''
* With the abbreviations
::<math>\begin{align}
M &:= {\color{blue} \frac 1 4} \left(\vec{SC}^2+\frac{1}{3}\vec{AB}^2 \right) \\
N &:= \frac{1}{{\color{blue}4}\sqrt{3}} \left|\det \left(\vec{SC},\vec{AB} \right)\right|
\end{align}</math>
:one gets for the [[Semi-major and semi-minor axes|semi-axes]] {{mvar|a, b}} (where {{math|''a'' > ''b''}}):
::<math>\begin{align}
a &= \frac{1}{2} \left(\sqrt{M+2N}+\sqrt{M-2N} \right) \\
b &= \frac{1}{2} \left(\sqrt{M+2N}-\sqrt{M-2N} \right)\ .
\end{align}</math>

* The '''linear eccentricity''' {{mvar|c}} of the Steiner inellipse is
::<math>c=\sqrt{a^2-b^2}=\dotsb=\sqrt{\sqrt{M^2-4N^2}}\ .</math>

==Trilinear equation==

The equation of the Steiner inellipse in [[trilinear coordinates]] for a triangle with side lengths {{mvar|a, b, c}} (with these parameters having a different meaning than previously) is<ref name=Weisstein/>
:<math>a^2x^2+b^2y^2+c^2z^2-2abxy-2bcyz-2cazx = 0</math>

where {{mvar|x}} is an arbitrary positive constant times the distance of a point from the side of length {{mvar|a}}, and similarly for {{mvar|b}} and {{mvar|c}} with the same multiplicative constant.

==Other properties==

The lengths of the semi-major and semi-minor axes for a triangle with sides {{mvar|a, b, c}} are<ref name=Weisstein/>

:<math>\frac{1}{6}\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2 \pm 2Z},</math>

where

:<math>Z=\sqrt{a^4+b^4+c^4-a^2b^2-b^2c^2-c^2a^2}.</math>

According to [[Marden's theorem]],<ref name=Kalman/> if the three [[Vertex (geometry)|vertices]] of the triangle are the [[complex number|complex]] [[polynomial#Solving polynomial equations|zeros]] of a cubic [[polynomial]], then the [[Focus (geometry)|foci]] of the Steiner inellipse are the zeros of the [[derivative]] of the polynomial.

The major axis of the Steiner inellipse is the [[Orthogonal regression|line of best orthogonal fit]] for the vertices.<ref name=Minda>{{citation
 | last1 = Minda | first1 = D. | author1-link = David Minda
 | last2 = Phelps | first2 = S.
 | issue = 8
 | journal = [[American Mathematical Monthly]]
 | mr = 2456092
 | pages = 679–689
 | title = Triangles, ellipses, and cubic polynomials
 | url = http://www.geogebra.org/en/upload/files/english/steve_phelps/minda%20phelps.pdf
 | volume = 115
 | year = 2008| doi = 10.1080/00029890.2008.11920581 }}.</ref>{{rp|Corollary 2.4}}

Denote the centroid and the first and second [[Fermat point]]s of a triangle as {{tmath|G,F_+,F_-}} respectively. The major axis of the triangle's Steiner inellipse is the inner bisector of {{tmath|\angle F_+GF_-.}} The lengths of the axes are <math>|GF_-| \pm |GF_+|\! ;</math> that is, the sum and difference of the distances of the Fermat points from the centroid.<ref name=Scimemi>[http://forumgeom.fau.edu/FG2010volume10/FG201008.pdf Scimemi, Benedetto, "Simple Relations Regarding the Steiner Inellipse of a Triangle", ''Forum Geometricorum'' 10, 2010: 55–77.]</ref>{{rp|Thm. 1}}

The axes of the Steiner inellipse of a triangle are tangent to its [[Kiepert conics|Kiepert parabola]], the unique parabola that is tangent to the sides of the triangle and has the [[Euler line]] as its [[Directrix (conic section)|directrix]].<ref name=Scimemi/>{{rp|Thm. 3}}

The foci of the Steiner inellipse of a triangle are the intersections of the inellipse's major axis and the circle with center on the minor axis and going through the Fermat points.<ref name=Scimemi/>{{rp|Thm. 6}}

As with any ellipse inscribed in a triangle {{math|△''ABC''}}, letting the foci be {{mvar|P}} and {{mvar|Q}} we have<ref>Allaire, Patricia R.; Zhou, Junmin; and Yao, Haishen, "Proving a nineteenth century ellipse identity", ''[[Mathematical Gazette]]'' 96, March 2012, 161-165.</ref>

:<math>\frac{\overline{PA} \cdot \overline{QA}}{\overline{CA} \cdot \overline{AB}} + \frac{\overline{PB} \cdot \overline{QB}}{\overline{AB} \cdot \overline{BC}} + \frac{\overline{PC} \cdot \overline{QC}}{\overline{BC} \cdot \overline{CA}} = 1.</math>

== Graphical construction ==
[[File:ConstruccionInelipseSteiner.png|thumb|400px|Graphical construction of the Steiner inellipse.
{{legend-line|solid #3366ff 2px|Given triangle {{math|△''ABC''}}}}
{{legend-line|dotted #6699ff 2px|Equilaterial triangle {{math|△''A'BC''}}}}
{{legend-line|dashed red 1px|Line segment {{mvar|{{overline|A'A}}}} and its perpendicular bisector}}
{{legend-line|dotted red 2px|Circle centered at {{mvar|O}}}}
{{legend-line|dotted green 2px|Rays {{math|{{overline|''k''{{sub|1}}''A''}}}} and {{math|{{overline|''k''{{sub|2}}''A''}}}}}}
{{legend-line|dashed red 3px|Steiner inellipse}}
]]

The Steiner inellipse of a triangle {{math|△''ABC''}} can be determined using a graphical construction based on establishing an [[affine transformation]] between the given triangle and an [[equilateral triangle]]. Since this projection preserves the midpoints of the sides, it allows for a graphical correspondence between the [[incircle]] of the equilateral triangle and the desired inellipse. The major and minor axes of an ellipse are always perpendicular. The construction uses a circle passing through {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|A'}} (the original and transformed vertices) to find specific points {{math|''k''{{sub|1}}}} and {{math|''k''{{sub|2}}}} on the axis of affinity. The rays {{math|{{overline|''k''{{sub|1}}''A''}}}} and {{math|{{overline|''k''{{sub|2}}''A''}}}} identify the unique directions that remain perpendicular after the transformation, which must be the directions of the ellipse's semi-axes.<ref name=IZQUIERDO>{{cite book |last=Izquierdo Asensi |first=Fernando |title=Geometría Descriptiva Superior y Aplicada |date=September 1975 |publisher=DOSSAT |isbn=8423704416 |page=123}}</ref>

To perform the construction, one side of the triangle is taken as the axis of affinity. (If the triangle is equilateral, the problem is trivial as the inellipse is its incircle; if it is isosceles, one of the two equal sides is typically chosen).

The procedure is as follows:
# Given {{math|△''ABC''}}, construct the equilateral triangle {{math|△''A'BC''}} on side {{mvar|BC}}.
# Draw the segment {{mvar|{{overline|A'A}}}} (the direction of affinity with axis {{mvar|BC}}) between the two triangles.
# From the midpoint {{mvar|m}} of {{mvar|{{overline|A'A}}}}, draw the [[perpendicular bisector]] until it intersects the line {{mvar|BC}} (or its extension) at point {{mvar|O}}.
# Draw the circle centered at {{mvar|O}} that passes through {{mvar|A'}} and {{mvar|A}}, which intersects the line {{mvar|BC}} at points {{math|''k''{{sub|1}}}} and {{math|''k''{{sub|2}}}}.
# The direction of the ray {{math|{{overline|''k''{{sub|1}}''A''}}}}  coincides with the major axis of the Steiner inellipse, and the ray {{math|{{overline|''k''{{sub|2}}''A''}}}}  with the minor axis.
# The endpoints of the semi-axes are obtained by projecting the points of the incircle of the equilateral triangle—specifically those where the tangents are parallel to rays {{math|{{overline|''k''{{sub|1}}''A' ''}}}} and {{math|{{overline|''k''{{sub|2}}''A' ''}}}} —it relies on the fact that affine transformations preserve parallelism between two lines in the same plane.

This same construction is applicable to the [[Steiner circumellipse]], but uses the [[circumcircle]] of the equilateral triangle instead of the incircle.

==Generalization==

The Steiner inellipse of a triangle can be generalized to {{mvar|n}}-gons: some {{mvar|n}}-gons have an interior ellipse that is tangent to each side at the side's midpoint. Marden's theorem still applies: the foci of the Steiner inellipse are zeroes of the derivative of the polynomial whose zeroes are the vertices of the {{mvar|n}}-gon.<ref>[http://forumgeom.fau.edu/FG2006volume6/FG200633.pdf Parish, James L., "On the derivative of a vertex polynomial", ''Forum Geometricorum'' 6, 2006, pp. 285–288: Proposition 5.]</ref>
